abstract: Ionic composition is a key determinant of ribosomal RNA structure and function. Metal cations such as potassium (K+) and magnesium (Mg2+) stabilize rRNA architecture. While certain positions in the ribosome are strictly occupied by either potassium or magnesium for distinct structural or functional reasons, their broader role in modulating ribosomal dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we use microsecond-scale coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of the bacterial 70S ribosome to examine how ionic composition affects structural flexibility and long-range communication. We compare a native ribosome with experimentally resolved ions to two variants: a magnesium-enriched model, in which K+ ions are replaced with Mg2+, and a hydrated magnesium model. While these substitutions do not aim to reproduce physiological ionic conditions, they provide a controlled framework to isolate the physical effects of ion identity on ribosomal dynamics. Increasing magnesium content reduces ionic and backbone mobility and enhances rigidity within the ribosomal core. Dynamic Flexibility Index analysis shows that these changes extend beyond local coordination sites, producing flexibility shifts at distances exceeding 30 Å. Dynamic Coupling Index analysis further reveals that ionic perturbations reshape long-range communication pathways. Functionally important regions, including the L1 and L7/12 stalks, exhibit distinct, ion-dependent responses, while the L10-L11 region shows enhanced long-range coupling under varying ionic conditions. These results demonstrate that ionic composition modulates both local stability and global ribosomal dynamics, with implications for translational efficiency and fidelity.
